data.title: Beyond Tolerance: The Mongols’ Religious Policies in Yuan-dynasty China and Il-khanate Iran, 1200-1368
data.abstractNote:
Since Edward Gibbons designated the Mongols as an example of perfect tolerance in the late nineteenth century, scholars have often repeated his idea that Mongols were one of the earliest example of religious tolerance. However, this study proves how misleading this view is.
In China, the Mongols introduced policies to incorporate multiple religious groups - including, but not limited to, the Christians, Buddhists, Daoists, Muslims, Dhuta sect and the White cloud sect - not because they were religiously tolerant, but because the Mongols benefited from supporting the religions. And accordingly each of the religious groups proactively responded and reacted to these policies. Moreover, policies towards the religious groups changed constantly depending on historical circumstances, the role of different religious figures, and the needs of the empire.
A close examination of the religious institutions within the Yuan government, tax exemption rules, and the joint court system in China clearly demonstrate that these seemingly tolerant policies resulted from ongoing negotiations and interactions between the Mongol empire and the religious groups, depending on the specific historical circumstances. The close reading of unedited governmental documents and inscriptions has enabled this study to present this new perspective. The Mongols in China wrote these governmental documents and inscriptions in a unique Mongolian-influenced Chinese style, and previously scholarship in English has not always examined these documents thoroughly due to this unique and difficult style. Incorporating these challenging and neglected sources has changed our understanding of the Mongols and the different religions under their rule.
In contrast to the Mongols in China, we have a rather different image of the Mongols in Iran. Most studies on the religion of the Il-Khanate have focused on the Islamization of the Mongols, and accordingly, we tend to think that Mongols in Iran were religiously intolerant and only favored Islam. This idea is mostly dues to the limitation of sources, and especially the key sources that have changed our understanding of religion in the Yuan barely survive for Il-Khanate Iran.
But a careful read of the Il-Khanate sources on religion, especially comparing the accounts of Christian authors with Muslims sources challenge this idea. We can see that the religious landscape of the Il-Khanate was much more diverse then we tend to think, as Christians and Buddhists flourished and held important positions within the Il-Khanate. Christians and Buddhists had skills to offer to the Il-Khans, and they were willing to cooperate to the Mongol, rule of Iran. Accordingly, the Il-Khans offered their support to these religions to facilitate their rule. Like the Yuan dynasty rulers in China, the Ilkhanate rulers did not announce a policy of tolerance that they tried to enforce. Instead they created policies for the different religions in their realms in response to specific, always changing circumstances, sometimes favoring members of one group, sometimes favoring another.
Tolerance, or the lack of tolerance, is not the best way for us to understand the Mongol empire's policies concerning religion. Imagining a religiously tolerant empire neglects the changing policies over time; it overlooks the importance of human actors and historical circumstances that prompted these changing policies. Focusing on the interactions among individuals, specific circumstances, and changes over time is the key to understanding the Mongol empire and religion. Through this examination, my study enriches our understanding of how the Mongols administered the religiously diverse empire, adds insight to comparative studies of empires, and contributes to the recent discussions surrounding the social history of religious tolerance.

data.abstractNote:
The first archaeological evidence for the complex of Khirbet el-Libneh was exposed in 1997 during development works that were carried out in the industrial zone of Tartous (on the Syrian coast). Indeed, the nine excavations carried out under the direction of the DGAM between 1998 and 2009, led to the partial discovery of an early Byzantine settlement. The remains, scattered over an area of 11,400 m², consist mainly of a large basilica decorated with geometric mosaics, sewers and basins connected to a cistern, a large agricultural complex and ancillary rooms. A wall of a considerable size flanks the eastern side of the site, thus implying that the site was protected by a wall.
Further surveys will be needed before we can portray a full picture of the complex and its contents. In the meantime, the available data serve as the source material of my PhD thesis. This article provides a general overview of the components and materials found on this site, and attempts to give an idea as to its function.

data.title: Une nouvelle collection d’écrits d’Isaac de Ninive
data.abstractNote: «Under the name of Isaac of Nineveh, or Isaac the Syrian, one of the best-known Syriac authors, different collections of spiritual homilies are preserved. To the First Collection, widely appreciated and translated in numerous languages from the 9th century on, have been added two other collections recently discovered: the Second and the Third. The last one, contained in a unique and recent manuscript preserved in Teheran (Issayi 5), has just been published and translated; it is briefly presented here. The 14 homilies that compose this manuscript contain themes typical of Isaac on the relations between ascetical practices and contemplation, prayer, divine mercy and the mildness of judgment. Two homilies consist entirely of prayers and two others are letters addressed to hermits facing difficulties, on the reasons for solitary life and on joy.» (p. 304)

data.abstractNote: The observation of certain similarities between some Muslim texts of the first generations Sufis and the Apophtegmata of the Fathers of the Egyptian desert raised the hypothesis that the Apophtegmata were known to these Sufis. Moreover, studies undertaken during the last decades on Muslim mystics brought to light certain similarities with the Christian ascetic world, both in the field of reflection as in practices. The present article would like to suggest some historical links illustrating these similarities. It is generally known that Muslim ascetics frequented Christian monasteries and interrogated the monks; sometimes mention is also made of books they read in the monasteries. The Apophtegmata, which Christians from Syria-Mesopotamia translated into Syriac, could be among these books read and meditated upon by the Sufis.

data.title: Isaac de Ninive et sa doctrine: entre solitude et communion
data.abstractNote: Isaac of Nineveh lived at a time (7th century) when the East Syrian Church to which he belonged was no longer in communion with the other Christian Churches. Nevertheless his spiritual teachings have, over the centuries, been warmly received throughout the Christian world. Isaac lived at a time when an important reform of monastic life in the East Syrian Church had been carried out under the leadership of Abraham of Kashkar, who sought to eliminate certain excesses. He sought to strike a balance between solitude and community in the life of the monk. Monks were to live alone in hermit-ages, but to come together in the main church for the Saturday night vigil service and the Sunday meal. For Isaac, in line with this tradition, the experience of solitude was the very condition of community life. Discernment was indispensable, if ascetic practice ― either in solitude or in community —was not to become an end in itself, or lose sight of its very goal. The monastic quest must not be pure introspection: a monk is mature for solitude when he is able to live a brotherly life with others. Through solitude he must learn to relate to God, to others and to himself. The goal of solitude is to find compassion — in charity and communion — for every creature and for all of creation. This must apply in particular to those who have distanced themselves from truth. True solitude is not self-seeking; it leads neither to judging others nor to bitterness, but to the fulness of charity.
